issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, where the patient is the victim rather than someone exposed to other victims. This trigger implies a different trauma context unless there is additional unreported trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is difficult to fit with the available profile for a 23-year-old single ship captain with childhood caregiver abuse, because no salient caregiving/protective role failure is otherwise represented in the triggers, threat, or memory content. It reads as a role-specific trauma appraisal from a different context rather than a coherent extension of the rest of this profile.

vignette:
Mai was twenty-three years old and the captain of a coastal cargo vessel, a job she had earned through years of relentless discipline and a fierce need to be in control. She had grown up in a small fishing town in Vietnam, the daughter of a fisherman whose anger was as constant as the tide. From the age of six until she left home at sixteen, her father would beat her with a leather strap whenever she made a mistake-spilling water, failing to clean fish quickly enough, speaking out of turn. He often locked her in a windowless storage closet for hours afterward, and she would sit in the absolute dark, listening to his footsteps fade, certain he would never come back. She learned to breathe shallowly, to stay perfectly still, to map the closet's dimensions with her fingers in case she needed to escape. What frightened her most was not the pain itself but the moment after the beating, when she was alone in the black and could not tell whether she was still alive or had become a ghost.

Now, aboard her ship, the darkness returned every night. She slept in a small cabin with a single porthole, but she always kept the curtain open so she could see the faint glow of the navigation lights. Waking in the middle of the night, disoriented, she would freeze, her heart pounding, before she remembered where she was. She had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that danger could appear from any shadow, and that her body had to stay ready. Every muscle was perpetually tense; her jaw ached from clenching. She could not relax, even when the sea was calm. Her crew-mostly men-respected her authority, but being alone with any of them in the engine room or the galley made her chest tight. She always positioned herself near the door, noting the quickest route to the deck. Before stepping into any space, she scanned for exits, windows, anything that could serve as an escape. Her crew noticed that she never stood with her back to a door and that she always walked along the outer edge of the bridge, as if she planned to jump overboard.

Driving was another problem. When she came ashore, she needed to drive supply trucks from the port to the depot, but she could not tolerate passengers. The presence of another person in the vehicle-especially a man-made her feel trapped, suffocated. She remembered her father driving her to the docks as a child, hitting her with his free hand while she sat in the passenger seat, unable to get out. Now, if a colleague offered a ride, she made excuses. She preferred to drive alone, even if it meant longer routes, because she could control every turn and stop. But even alone, her mind raced with imagined threats: a car cutting her off, a breakdown in a solitary stretch of road. She felt isolated, set apart from everyone her age. Other young people went to parties, dated, lived in shared apartments. Mai lived on her ship or in a rented room near the port, and she had no close friends. She believed there was something wrong with her as a person-a defect that others could sense, a reason her father had treated her the way he did.

The consequences had accumulated quietly over two years. She had turned down a promotion that would have required her to train junior officers because the job involved sitting in a small classroom with male trainees. Her social life had evaporated; she spent her days off alone in her room, watching the door. She had started drinking-not heavily, but enough to dull the edge of tension in the evenings. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment on the bridge last month: a male crew member touched her shoulder to get her attention at night, and she spun around, her fist raised, before she could stop herself. The look of shock on his face-and her own shame-convinced her she could not go on this way. She came to the clinic hoping that someone could help her feel less afraid, though she was equally terrified that talking about the closet would make the darkness inside her grow worse.
